findings.text: Two generic helpers are visible beyond their file, named kvm_range_has_memory_attributes for interval uniformity queries and kvm_use_dirty_bitmap for dirty-mode queries, supported by kvm_get_memory_attributes for single-frame reads.

The x86 side exposes kvm_arch_prepare_memory_region for validation and kvm_arch_commit_memory_region for propagation and kvm_arch_free_memslot for release and kvm_mmu_change_mmu_pages for cache sizing.

Slot tracking exposes kvm_page_track_create_memslot with kvm_page_track_free_memslot and kvm_page_track_delete_slot for lifecycle, plus memslot_rmap_alloc for reverse maps and kvm_mmu_init_memslot_memory_attributes for attribute seeding.

During a slot change the generic flow enters architecture code at two points. The first entry runs before installation and may veto the change while producing fresh metadata. The second entry runs after accounting updates and handles tracker notification, cache sizing, flag propagation and retirement of prior arrays.

Two additional entries serve queries and resource control. The attribute-range entry answers uniformity questions over many frames with read-side protection. The cache-size entry is invoked when total slot pages change and no explicit cache size was requested, driving reclamation of older paging structures.

Slot updates proceed through guarded stages. A dedicated mutex is taken first. Removal or relocation first swaps in a temporary invalid view so processors keep running without encountering missing mappings. Preparation then runs. On success a change-specific installer records the outcome and the temporary view is discarded before commit. On preparation failure the invalid view is rolled back for removal or relocation, otherwise the mutex is simply released.

Preparation normalizes dirty tracking state for every change except removal. Disabling the logging flag clears the new bitmap reference so the old storage can be freed later. Keeping logging enabled reuses the prior bitmap when one exists. Enabling logging afresh allocates new storage when bitmap mode is active, optionally marking every page dirty when manual protection with initial set is configured. Allocation failures abort preparation and release any freshly allocated bitmap.

The x86 preparation step enforces slot placement rules. Relocation is refused while external tracking consumers are attached. Creation and relocation are refused when the last frame exceeds the paging limit or collides with a direct-access alias. Successful creation or relocation then builds architecture metadata. Flag-only updates inherit prior architecture state while removal needs no work.

The highest mappable guest frame derives from host address width. When translated paging is active the host maximum width is used, otherwise a 52-bit fallback applies. The bound is the width shifted down by page size exponent minus one, preventing installation of entries the host cannot address.

Whether a frame is treated as a direct-access alias is decided by masking the frame number with per-virtual-machine direct bits. A nonzero overlap means alias, zero means ordinary. The direct bits value is stored in the architecture portion of the virtual machine object.

Fresh architecture metadata starts cleared so relocation never inherits stale pointers. Reverse-mapping arrays are built when the virtual machine uses them. Large-page descriptors are then allocated for every huge level above the base page. Edge descriptors are marked unusable when slot boundaries split a huge page, and an entire level is marked unusable when guest and userspace alignment disagree. Attribute markers and write-tracking storage are seeded last, with any failure releasing all partial allocations.

When private memory is supported, slot creation scans each fully contained huge page at every level from the smallest huge size upward. Fully uniform pages have their mixed marker cleared, others have it set. Uniformity at the smallest huge size is decided by a range query; larger sizes recurse through their children and also consult per-frame attributes, treating any mixed child or differing value as mixed.

Per-frame memory attributes live in an indexed array keyed by frame number, with missing entries meaning no attributes. Lookup converts the stored entry to a value, yielding zero when absent. Only the private attribute is advertised as supported when the architecture offers private memory, otherwise no attributes are supported. Range checks first intersect the requested mask with supported bits and reject any requested bits outside that intersection.

Multi-frame attribute queries hold read-side protection and examine each index individually because absent entries invalidate iterator position. The scan retries on concurrent internal marks, treats a missing entry as success only when seeking zero attributes, warns if a present entry decodes to zero, and fails when position drifts or masked value differs. A single-frame range uses a direct lookup fast path.

Write-tracking storage is created only when that feature is enabled for the virtual machine. Creation allocates one small record per frame on first use and keeps existing storage on later calls. Failure to allocate is reported as out of memory, success leaves a usable per-frame array.

Reverse-mapping storage consists of one array per paging level sized to the number of large pages in the slot. Allocation skips levels that already have storage and on any failure releases every level and reports out of memory. Release walks all levels, freeing each array and clearing its pointer.

Dirty bitmap extent is derived from the slot page count rounded up to machine word granularity and expressed in bytes. Allocation reserves twice that extent, providing space for a pair of bitmaps. Destruction is a no-op for empty references and otherwise frees storage and clears the reference.

Commit first adjusts the virtual-machine page total for creation and removal so architecture code observes the new total, and nudges the dirty-logging slot count when the logging flag changes state. Architecture commit then runs. Creation needs no further work. Removal frees the slot and its metadata. Relocation and flag-only paths free the old bitmap when logging stopped, detach any guest memory binding, and free the detached shell without touching reused metadata.

The x86 commit step notifies tracking consumers on removal, grows or shrinks the paging cache in proportion to total slot pages with a minimum floor when no explicit size was requested, propagates flag effects into paging structures, and on relocation frees the architecture arrays belonging to the retired slot.

Cache resizing takes write exclusion. When current usage exceeds the goal, inactive paging roots are reclaimed oldest first while skipping structures still referenced as roots. Each candidate is prepared for removal into a batch list, with unstable walks restarting from the beginning. The batch is then committed, recycled statistics advance, and the allowed maximum is updated to the achieved level.

Presence of external page-tracking consumers is reported by testing whether the notifier list is empty. One build configuration performs that list test, another configuration always reports absent, allowing the same call sites to compile with tracking disabled.

Frame rounding for a paging level clears the low bits that index inside a huge page, yielding the containing huge-page base. Manual dirty-log state is read from a per-virtual-machine mask testing a dedicated initial-set bit. Bitmap mode is active whenever no ring is configured or the ring is explicitly paired with a bitmap.

Slot removal notification iterates external consumers under sleepable read protection and invokes each registered removal callback with base and length, doing nothing when no consumers exist. A disabled-tracking build provides an empty notification. Architecture release frees reverse maps, large-page descriptors and write-tracking storage, clearing each pointer.

The mutex named slots_arch_lock serializes installation of new slot tables. It is acquired before copying current tables and held until new tables are published, then released before waiting for readers. Code mutating slots without the outer lock must acquire this mutex before reading the table pointer and hold it until mutations finish.
Deciding bitmap dirty mode requires holding the outer lock named slots_lock. The check reads ring size with ring-with-bitmap configuration, and a debug assertion enforces the precondition.
Adjusting the paging-cache goal requires write exclusion on the lock named mmu_lock. Usage comparison with oldest-first reclamation and maximum update all occur under that exclusion.

Attribute range scans run under read-side protection that tolerates concurrent array updates via retry. Removal notification holds sleepable read protection across the consumer walk, relying on that mechanism rather than on exclusive locking.

Observed slot state includes base_gfn with npages and flags and dirty_bitmap and userspace_addr, plus an arch area with rmap with lpage_info with gfn_write_track. Descriptors carry disallow_lpage including a mixed bit.

Observed machine state includes slots_arch_lock with slots_lock with mmu_lock and nr_memslot_pages with nr_memslots_dirty_logging and manual_dirty_log_protect with dirty_ring_size with dirty_ring_with_bitmap and mem_attr_array and gfn_direct_bits with n_requested_mmu_pages with n_max_mmu_pages and active_mmu_pages with track_notifier_head.

Observed paging nodes carry root_count with link for age order. Consumers link through track_notifier_list with track_srcu and optionally provide track_remove_region receiving base with length. Statistics record mmu_shadow_pages with mmu_recycled.

Each slot change moves through distinct phases. Removal and relocation start in temporary invalidation, all changes enter preparation, then diverge to creation, removal, relocation or flag-only installation, and converge on commit with accounting and cleanup. Preparation failure returns to the prior state, restoring the original view for removal and relocation.

Dirty-logging state follows flag edges. Turning logging on allocates or reuses a bitmap and increments the global logging count. Keeping it on preserves the bitmap across changes. Turning it off detaches the bitmap for later release and decrements the count. Ring-only configurations suppress bitmap allocation entirely.

The paging-cache size controller rests at its goal while usage stays below it. Exceeding the goal triggers oldest-first eviction until usage meets the target or no evictable pages remain, then the goal is latched to the achieved usage. Growth of slot memory raises the goal automatically unless an explicit size was requested.

Relocation is unsafe with external tracking consumers and is rejected. Guest-memory-backed slots are never relocatable and flag-only updates on them are treated as unexpected, with runtime checks flagging violations. Unbinding of guest memory occurs on the retired slot after the new binding exists.

An unrecognized change selector is treated as a fatal programming error in both installation and commit paths. After the architecture slot mutex is released, the caller-supplied architecture view may be stale and architectures must tolerate that. Allocation failures during preparation abort the change and must unwind any partial bitmap or metadata.

Installing mappings beyond the host-addressable limit or onto alias addresses would create entries that faults cannot service correctly, so such creations and relocations are refused. Huge pages that straddle slot edges, misalign guest versus userspace, or span differing attributes are suppressed to avoid incorrect large mappings.

The slot-change vocabulary provides four distinct operations for creation, removal, relocation and flag-only update, named KVM_MR_CREATE and KVM_MR_DELETE and KVM_MR_MOVE and KVM_MR_FLAGS_ONLY. Preparation, installation and commit each distinguish among these cases.

Observed control names include KVM_MEM_LOG_DIRTY_PAGES for dirty tracking and KVM_MEM_GUEST_MEMFD for guest-memory backing and KVM_MEMORY_ATTRIBUTE_PRIVATE for private state and KVM_DIRTY_LOG_INITIALLY_SET for initial dirty marking. Extent math relies on word and page granularity.

Observed sizing names include KVM_NR_PAGE_SIZES and PG_LEVEL_2M and KVM_MAX_HUGEPAGE_LEVEL and KVM_PAGES_PER_HPAGE and KVM_LPAGE_MIXED_FLAG and KVM_MEMSLOT_PAGES_TO_MMU_PAGES_RATIO and KVM_MIN_ALLOC_MMU_PAGES, covering level counts and huge bounds and per-level counts and mixed marking and cache sizing.
